notes.meaning: The Lord gave these instructions directly to Moses as the leader of Israel. After giving laws about clean and unclean animals, God turned to ceremonial uncleanness that comes from within human bodies. This began a new section teaching Israel how to stay ritually pure before a holy God.

A mother who gave birth to a boy was considered ceremonially unclean for seven days, just as she was during her monthly period. Being unclean did not mean that having a baby was a moral sin, because children are a blessing from God. Instead, the loss of blood and bodily fluids made her temporarily unfit to touch holy things.

On the eighth day after his birth, the baby boy was circumcised. Circumcision was the physical mark of God's special covenant promise given to Abraham and his descendants. This took place right after the mother's first week of separation ended, when the infant was ready for the covenant sign.

For thirty-three days after the first week, making forty days in total, the mother remained at home in a second stage of cleansing. She could not enter the sacred courtyard of the tabernacle or eat holy food from offerings. This time gave her quiet days to heal and regain strength before returning to public worship.

If a woman gave birth to a daughter, the purification time was doubled to two weeks of initial separation and sixty-six days of gradual cleansing, totaling eighty days. Commentators note that this difference may have honored the male rite of circumcision on the eighth day, or reflected ancient ideas about physical recovery. Above all, it rested on God's sovereign command for Israel's life of worship.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that two weeks was the natural length of heavy bleeding after childbirth, but the period was shortened for a son so he could be circumcised on the eighth day.

notes.meaning: When her days of purification ended, the mother brought two animals to the priest at the tabernacle entrance. She offered a year-old lamb as a burnt offering to show devotion to God, and a pigeon or turtledove as a sin offering to be ritually cleansed. This ceremony was for the mother herself to welcome her back into worship, not because the newborn child was unholy.

The priest offered these sacrifices on the altar to make atonement for her, which here means making her ritually clean and ready for worship. God declared her cleansed from the flow of blood that had set her apart. This rule applied equally to every mother, whether she had given birth to a boy or a girl.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view this sin offering as cleansing the tabernacle from physical defilement rather than forgiving personal guilt, since the text promises the woman will be clean rather than forgiven.

notes.meaning: If a family was too poor to buy a lamb, God kindly allowed the mother to bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons instead. One bird replaced the lamb for the burnt offering, and the other was used for the sin offering. This rule ensured that poverty never kept anyone away from God, and it was the very offering brought by Mary after the birth of Jesus.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Mary observed this purification law forty days after the birth of Christ out of humble obedience to the law, even though giving birth to the Savior involved no sin or moral fault.
